### Deep & Tricky

**DT-55. In "max sum ≤ k" problems, the answer may not exist (every rectangle exceeds k), and returning 0 or −∞ silently differs from the problem's convention; likewise, in "max points on a line", duplicates of the anchor lie on every line through it and must be added to every bucket, not counted as a direction.** *(Specification edge cases)* Hard problems are hard largely because of such cases: empty answers, duplicates, ties, and degenerate inputs. The brute forces in this chapter handle them by definition, which is why every coded problem here was stress-tested on tiny ranges where those cases are common.

## Topic 47B — The problem cards

## Unit 47.4 — Cards 13–56: arrays, strings, search, data structures

Each card: **signals** → **insight** → **algorithm, complexity** → *trap* → where the template lives.

**13. Median of two sorted arrays** — "sorted", "O(log(m+n))" → binary-search the partition of the shorter array so left halves together hold half the elements → O(log min) → *off-by-one with empty sides; use ±∞ sentinels* → Unit 6.4.
**14. K-th smallest in a sorted matrix** — rows and columns sorted → binary search on the value, count ≤ mid by a staircase walk → O(n log V) → *the answer must be an element: search on values, return lo* → Ch. 6.
**15. Find the duplicate number (no modification, O(1) memory)** — values in [1, n], n + 1 of them → Floyd's cycle detection on i → a[i] → O(n) → *index 0 is the tail entry* → DT-15.
**16. First missing positive** — O(n) time, O(1) space → cyclic sort: place v at index v − 1 → O(n) → *loop with `while`, guard duplicates* → Unit 2.6.
**17. Trapping rain water (1-D)** — "water between bars" → two pointers moving the smaller side, or a monotonic stack → O(n) → *level is bounded by the lower side* → Ch. 4.
**18. Largest rectangle in histogram** — "maximal area of bars" → monotonic stack: width between previous and next smaller → O(n) → *sentinel 0 to flush* → Unit 9.3.
**19. Maximal rectangle of 1s** — binary matrix → histogram per row → O(RC) → *reset heights at 0* → Ch. 9 project.
**20. Sliding window maximum** — "max of each window" → monotonic deque of indices → O(n) → *pop expired from the front first* → Unit 5.5.
**21. Minimum window substring** — "smallest window containing all of t" → variable window with a "missing" counter → O(n) → *shrink while valid, record before shrinking* → Ch. 5.
**22. Subarrays with exactly K distinct** — "exactly k" → atMost(k) − atMost(k − 1) → O(n) → *direct window for "exactly" is wrong* → Unit 5.3.
**23. Shortest subarray with sum ≥ K, negatives allowed** — negatives break windows → prefix sums + increasing deque → O(n) → *pop front when satisfied, back when dominated* → Unit 9.4.
**24. Count of range sum** — "number of subarrays with sum in [lo, hi]" → prefix sums + merge-sort counting or Fenwick → O(n log n) → *inclusive bounds* → Units 19.2, 41.1.
**25. Count of smaller numbers after self** — "for each element, how many to its right are smaller" → right-to-left with Fenwick over ranks → O(n log n) → *equal values are not smaller* → Ch. 14 project, Unit 19.2.
**26. Reverse pairs (a[i] > 2a[j])** — pair counting with a non-monotone-looking condition → merge sort, two pointers across halves → O(n log n) → *floor division with negatives* → Unit 41.1.
**27. Longest consecutive sequence** — "unsorted", "O(n)" → hash set, start counting only at sequence starts → O(n) → *starting at every element is O(n²)* → Ch. 3.
**28. Longest duplicate substring** — "repeated substring", n ≤ 3·10⁴ → binary search on length + rolling hash (verify), or suffix array → O(n log n) → *hash collisions* → Ch. 3 project, Ch. 39 project.
**29. Shortest palindrome by adding characters in front** — "longest palindromic prefix" → prefix function of `s + '#' + reverse(s)` → O(n) → *separator needed* → Unit 39.1.
**30. Palindrome pairs** — "concatenation is a palindrome" → hash map of reversed words; split each word into prefix/suffix, check palindromic parts → O(n·L²) → *empty string and the word itself* → Ch. 3.
**31. Text justification** — formatting rules → greedy line filling, distribute spaces left-heavy → O(total length) → *last line left-justified, single-word lines* → simulation.
**32. Basic calculator with + − ( ) and unary minus** — expression evaluation → stack of signs, or two stacks with precedence → O(n) → *unary minus after '('* → Unit 9.5.
**33. Decode string k[...]** — nesting → stack of (prefix, count) → O(output) → *multi-digit counts* → Unit 9.1.
**34. Remove duplicate letters (smallest lexicographic, each letter once)** — "smallest subsequence" → monotonic stack with "letter appears later" counts and an in-stack set → O(n) → *never pop a letter that does not appear later* → Unit 9.3 (remove k digits).
**35. Create maximum number from two arrays** — choose k digits preserving order → for each split i + (k − i), max subsequence of each via monotonic stack, then greedy merge comparing remaining suffixes → O(k·(m + n)²) → *merge must compare whole suffixes, not single digits* → Ch. 9.
**36. Sliding window median** — window order statistics → two heaps with lazy deletion, or SortedList → O(n log k) → *balance bookkeeping after lazy deletions* → Ch. 15 project.
**37. Data stream as disjoint intervals** — online insertions of points → ordered map of interval starts; merge with neighbours → O(log n) per add → *joining two intervals at once* → Ch. 38.
**38. Range module (add/remove/query ranges)** — online interval set → sorted list of boundaries with parity, or a dynamic segment tree → O(log n) amortised → *half-open endpoints* → Ch. 38 project.
**39. My calendar III (max k-booking)** — online overlap maximum → dynamic segment tree with range add + global max → O(log T) → *never-pushed tags* → Ch. 38 project.
**40. LFU cache** — O(1) eviction by frequency then recency → frequency buckets of ordered dicts + min-frequency → O(1) → *min_freq resets to 1 on insert* → Unit 43.2.
**41. All O(1) data structure (inc/dec/getMax/getMin keys)** — O(1) for everything → doubly linked list of count buckets, map key → bucket → O(1) → *remove empty buckets* → Ch. 43.
**42. Insert/delete/getRandom O(1) with duplicates** — random access + deletion → array + map value → set of indices; swap-with-last → O(1) → *update the moved element's index set* → Unit 43.3.
**43. Max frequency stack** — pop the most frequent, ties most recent → map freq → stack, max freq counter → O(1) → *push to every level up to its frequency* → Ch. 43.
**44. Serialise and deserialise a binary tree** — tree ↔ string → preorder with null markers → O(n) → *consume tokens with an iterator* → Unit 13.5.
**45. Binary tree maximum path sum** — "any path" → return one branch, record bent path → O(n) → *negative branches clipped at 0, node itself mandatory* → Unit 13.2.
**46. Vertical order traversal with ties by value** — coordinates → collect (col, row, val), sort → O(n log n) → *tie-break rules* → Ch. 13 project.
**47. Recover a BST with two swapped nodes** — inorder must be increasing → find the first and last inversions in inorder → O(n) (Morris for O(1) space) → *adjacent swap gives one inversion* → Unit 14.1.
**48. Count of smaller BST insertions / k-th smallest with updates** — order statistics under updates → treap or SortedList → O(log n) → *duplicates* → Unit 14.4.
**49. Word search II** — many words in a grid → trie + DFS with pruning → O(cells · 4^L) worst, fast in practice → *remove found words to avoid repeats* → Unit 16.2.
**50. Maximum XOR with an element from array (offline with limits)** — XOR + "≤ m" constraints → sort queries by m, insert numbers into a binary trie as m grows → O((n + q)·B) → *query on an empty trie* → Units 16.3, DT-54.
**51. Stream of characters (does any word end here?)** — suffix queries online → trie of reversed words, or Aho–Corasick → O(L) per char → *keep only the last max-length characters* → Unit 16.4.
**52. Number of islands II (online land additions)** — growing connectivity → DSU with component counter → O(α(n)) per op → *the same cell added twice* → Unit 17.4.
**53. Evaluate division** — ratios between variables → weighted DSU or BFS → O(α) per query → *unknown variables return −1* → Unit 17.3.
**54. Range sum query 2-D mutable** — 2-D point updates, rectangle sums → 2-D Fenwick → O(log R log C) → *inclusive ranges* → Ch. 19.
**55. Falling squares / skyline heights online** — range assign max, range max → segment tree with coordinate compression → O(n log n) → *half-open square sides* → Ch. 18.
**56. Count of distinct elements in ranges (offline)** — "distinct in [l, r]" → sort by r, last-occurrence marks in a Fenwick → O((n + q) log n) → *write answers back in query order* → Ch. 19 project.

## Unit 47.5 — Cards 57–100: graphs, DP, greedy, math, advanced

**57. Word ladder II (all shortest transformations)** — "all shortest paths" → BFS layers recording parents, then DFS back from the target → O(N·L·26 + output) → *build parents only from the previous layer* → Unit 20.5.
**58. Alien dictionary** — sorted words in unknown alphabet → first differing letters → edges → topological sort → O(total chars) → *prefix before longer word is invalid* → Unit 21.4.
**59. Course schedule III** — durations and deadlines → sort by deadline + max-heap, drop the longest when late → O(n log n) → *exchange argument* → Unit 37.2.
**60. Longest increasing path in a matrix** — "strictly increasing moves" → DAG on cells; memoised DFS or topological order by value → O(RC) → *recursion depth: use iterative order* → Ch. 21.
**61. Parallel courses with k per semester (n ≤ 15)** — tiny n, prerequisites, capacity → bitmask DP over taken courses, choose submasks of available of size ≤ k → O(3ⁿ) → *greedy by out-degree is wrong* → Unit 33.3.
**62. Network delay time** — "time for signal to reach all" → Dijkstra, answer = max distance → O(E log V) → *unreachable → −1* → Unit 22.1.
**63. Cheapest flights within k stops** — edge-count limit → Bellman–Ford with k + 1 rounds using the previous round's copy → O(k·E) → *no copy = too many edges* → Unit 22.3.
**64. Path with minimum effort (min max step)** — bottleneck path → Dijkstra on max, binary search + BFS, or DSU → O(RC log RC) → *distance is a max, not a sum* → Unit 46.1.
**65. Minimum cost to make at least one valid path** — arrows cost 0 to follow, 1 to change → 0-1 BFS → O(RC) → *push front for 0 edges* → Unit 22.2.
**66. Shortest path in grid with obstacle elimination** — "remove at most k" → BFS over (r, c, k left) with dominance → O(RCk) → *Manhattan shortcut when k is large* → Ch. 20 project.
**67. Shortest path to get all keys** — keys and locks on a grid → BFS over (r, c, key mask) → O(RC·2^K) → *lock check uses the current mask* → Units 20.5, 33.2.
**68. Swim in rising water** — earliest time with a path → three combinations → O(n² log n) → *start cell's own height* → Unit 46.1.
**69. Critical connections** — "removal disconnects" → bridges via low-links → O(V + E) → *parallel edges: skip by edge id* → Unit 24.2.
**70. Minimum number of edges to make a graph strongly connected** — condensation → max(sources, sinks), 0 if one SCC → O(V + E) → *single-SCC special case* → Unit 24.1.
**71. Reconstruct itinerary** — use every ticket once, lexicographically smallest → Hierholzer with sorted adjacency → O(E log E) → *greedy walk can get stuck; output is reversed post-order* → Unit 27.1.
**72. Cracking the safe** — every n-digit code as a substring → de Bruijn via Euler circuit → O(kⁿ) → *start with n − 1 zeros* → Unit 27.2.
**73. Find the shortest superstring** — n ≤ 12 strings → remove contained strings; Held–Karp on overlaps → O(2ⁿ·n²) → *reconstruct with parents* → Ch. 27 project.
**74. Maximum students taking an exam (no cheating)** — grid rows ≤ 8 wide → row-mask DP with compatibility between consecutive rows → O(R·4^C) → *broken seats* → Unit 33.5.
**75. Number of ways to wear different hats** — 40 hats, 10 people → DP over hats with a mask of **people** (the small dimension) → O(40·2¹⁰·10) → *choose the mask over the smaller set* → Ch. 33.
**76. Count vowels permutation / knight dialer** — fixed transitions, n steps → DP or matrix power for huge n → O(n) or O(log n) → *mod after each add* → Unit 36.5.
**77. Number of digit one** — count 1s in [1, n] → digit DP or per-position formula → O(log n) → *tight bound on the current digit* → Ch. 34.
**78. Numbers with repeated digits ≤ n** — complement: count numbers with all distinct digits → digit DP with mask and started → O(10·2¹⁰·log n) → *leading zeros* → Unit 34.2.
**79. Burst balloons** — product of neighbours → interval DP on the **last** balloon → O(n³) → *first-burst recurrence is wrong* → Unit 31.2, DT-39.
**80. Minimum cost to merge stones (k at a time)** — merging adjacent piles k at a time → interval DP with "merged into m piles" → O(n³/k) → *feasibility: (n − 1) % (k − 1) == 0* → Ch. 31.
**81. Palindrome partitioning II** — minimum cuts → palindrome table + 1-D DP → O(n²) → *O(n³) if the palindrome check is not precomputed* → Unit 31.3.
**82. Distinct subsequences** — count ways t appears in s → 2-D DP, 1-D backwards → O(nm) → *iterate j backwards* → Unit 29.4.
**83. Edit distance / one edit away** — minimum operations → 2-D DP; for "one away", a linear two-pointer scan → O(nm) / O(n) → *insert vs delete symmetry* → Unit 29.3.
**84. Interleaving string** — s3 from s1 and s2 preserving order → 2-D boolean DP → O(nm) → *length check first* → Unit 29.4.
**85. Russian doll envelopes** — 2-D nesting → sort by width asc, height desc; LIS on heights → O(n log n) → *descending tie-break* → Unit 29.2.
**86. Partition to k equal-sum subsets** — n ≤ 16 → backtracking with symmetry pruning, or bitmask DP of (filled buckets, fill) → O(2ⁿ·n) → *sort descending* → Ch. 10 project, Unit 33.1.
**87. Target sum (+/−)** — signs to reach S → subset with sum (total + S)/2 → counting knapsack → O(n·total) → *parity and zeros* → Ch. 30.
**88. Profitable schemes** — people budget, profit ≥ P → 0/1 knapsack in two dimensions, cap profit at P → O(n·G·P) → *"at least P" collapses all larger profits into P* → Unit 30.4.
**89. Stone game variants** — optimal play on a row → score-difference interval DP → O(n²) → *difference formulation avoids tracking turns* → Unit 31.4.
**90. Can I win (choose from 1..n, reach total)** — game state = set of used numbers → memoised win/lose over bitmasks → O(2ⁿ·n) → *pre-check: sum of 1..n < total* → Unit 35.3.
**91. Knight probability / new 21 game** — probability over steps → forward probability DP; sliding window sum for New 21 → O(n·k) → O(n) → *stop drawing at K* → Unit 35.1.
**92. IPO (maximise capital)** — projects unlocked by capital → sort by capital, max-heap of profits → O(n log n) → *stop when nothing affordable* → Unit 15.5.
**93. Minimum cost to hire k workers** — ratio sets the rate → sort by ratio, max-heap of qualities → O(n log n) → *exact ratios* → Unit 46.5.
**94. Jump game II / video stitching** — fewest jumps or clips → reach frontier greedy → O(n) → *layer boundaries* → Unit 37.3, H4.
**95. Candy** — neighbour constraints → two passes → O(n) → *take the max of both passes* → Unit 37.3.
**96. Queue reconstruction by height** — (h, k) pairs → sort by h desc, k asc; insert at index k → O(n²) or O(n log n) with an order-statistic tree → *taller people placed first are unaffected* → Ch. 14.
**97. Max points on a line** — gcd-normalised directions → O(n²) → *duplicates, vertical lines* → H10.
**98. Erect the fence (convex hull with collinear points)** — hull keeping boundary points → monotone chain with `< 0` pops → O(n log n) → *all-collinear input* → Unit 40.3.
**99. Self crossing (spiral path)** — "does the path cross itself" → only three local cases (4th, 5th, 6th segment interactions) → O(n) → *the 5-segment overlap case* → geometry casework.
**100. Split array into k parts minimising the largest sum** — "minimise the maximum" → binary search on the answer with a greedy counter, or DP with divide-and-conquer optimisation → O(n log S) → *lower bound = max element* → Units 6.3, 36.3.

### Pattern

**P-48. When you meet a new hard problem, write its card: signals → insight → algorithm and complexity → trap → closest template. If you cannot fill "insight", you have not solved it yet — return to the brute force and look for the structure the brute force wastes.** *(Practice)* Keep your own deck of cards; the act of compressing a solution into four lines is what makes it recognisable next time. *Trade-off:* cards help recall, but only implementation under time pressure builds reliability — code at least one problem per card family each week.

### Mastery check

1. **Predict.** Why does the Dijkstra-like heap in H1 (rain water II) process boundary cells in increasing order of *level*, not height?
2. **Predict.** For H8 (egg drop), how many moves are needed with 1 egg and 100 floors, and with 2 eggs and 100 floors?

## Chapter 47 Project — Timed drill

**Goal:** turn the cards into a timed self-test: the program picks 10 random cards (seeded, so you can repeat a set), prints only the problem names, and waits — you write signals, insight, and complexity for each; then the program prints the cards for comparison. Run it weekly with a new seed and log your score.

```python
# file: drill/drill.py
```

## Answers to the Chapter 47 prediction questions

**47.5 Q1.** A cell's water level is determined by the lowest wall on the best escape route, which may be a tall cell already raised to its level — so the frontier must be ordered by that effective level (`max(level, height)`), exactly like Dijkstra ordering by tentative distance.

**47.5 Q2.** 1 egg: 100 moves (try every floor bottom-up). 2 eggs: 14 moves, since f(m, 2) = m(m + 1)/2 ≥ 100 first holds at m = 14 — the program prints the value.

# Chapter 48 — Interview Craft: Communication, Testing, Complexity, Follow-ups

*Goal: perform in a coding interview the way this book has trained you to work — clarify, propose a brute force, improve it with a named pattern, code cleanly, test deliberately, analyse complexity precisely, and handle follow-ups about scale, streaming, and memory — including the "system-design-flavoured" DSA questions where data does not fit in memory.*

**What you will be able to do after this chapter**

- Run a 45-minute interview with a clear structure, thinking aloud usefully.
- Test your own code by hand with a small, deliberate set of cases — the interview version of stress testing.
- State time and space complexity precisely, including amortised and expected bounds.
- Answer the standard follow-ups: larger input, a stream, limited memory, many queries, concurrency.
- Sort and aggregate data larger than memory (external merge sort) and explain the I/O cost.

## Topic 48A — The interview itself

## Unit 48.1 — A structure for 45 minutes

**One-line summary:** Spend the time in five phases: **clarify** (2–5 min: inputs, constraints, edge cases, expected output), **plan** (5–10 min: brute force with its complexity, then the improved idea with its invariant — agree on it before coding), **code** (15–20 min: clean, named helpers, no premature micro-optimisation), **test** (5 min: walk through a normal case, then edge cases; fix bugs calmly), **analyse and extend** (5 min: complexity, follow-ups).

| Phase | What to say | Signals the interviewer looks for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clarify | "Can the array be empty? Are values negative? Is the input sorted? How large is n?" | Precision; not assuming |
| Plan | "Brute force is O(n²) by checking every pair. We can do O(n) with a hash map of complements, because…" | Pattern recognition; trade-offs |
| Code | Narrate the structure, not every keystroke: "this loop maintains the window invariant…" | Fluency; readable code |
| Test | "Let me trace [2, 7, 11] with target 9… and the empty case, and duplicates." | Ownership of correctness |
| Analyse | "O(n) time, O(n) space; with sorted input, two pointers give O(1) space." | Depth; awareness of alternatives |

**Thinking aloud** is not narration of typing; it is sharing **decisions**: what you considered, why you chose it, what you are unsure about. When stuck, say what you know ("this smells like a monotonic stack because we need the next smaller element") and try a tiny example by hand — interviewers routinely give hints to candidates who make their reasoning visible.

## Unit 48.2 — Testing without a computer

**One-line summary:** In an interview you cannot run 2,000 random tests, but you can choose the cases a stress test would find: **empty / single element**, **all equal**, **already sorted / reverse sorted**, **negative numbers and zero**, **duplicates**, **the extremes of each constraint**, and **one case that exercises every branch**. Trace the code on them line by line, tracking variables in a small table.

```python
# file: edge_cases.py
"""Generate the 'interview edge cases' for array problems, and show they catch typical bugs."""
def edge_cases(lo=-3, hi=3):
    yield []
    yield [lo]
    yield [0]
    yield [hi] * 4                                    # all equal
    yield list(range(lo, hi + 1))                     # sorted
    yield list(range(hi, lo - 1, -1))                 # reverse sorted
    yield [lo, hi, lo, hi]                            # duplicates, alternating
    yield [0, lo, 0, hi, 0]                           # zeros and signs

def max_subarray(a):                                  # correct Kadane (non-empty subarray)
    best = cur = a[0]
    for x in a[1:]:
        cur = max(x, cur + x)
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

def buggy_reset_at_zero(a):                           # common bug: reset when cur < 0, init best = 0
    best = cur = 0
    for x in a:
        cur = max(0, cur + x)
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

def brute(a):
    return max(sum(a[i:j]) for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(i + 1, len(a) + 1))

for case in edge_cases():
    if not case:
        continue                                       # this problem requires a non-empty array: say so!
    if buggy_reset_at_zero(case) != brute(case):
        print(f"edge case {case} exposes the bug: buggy={buggy_reset_at_zero(case)}, correct={brute(case)}")
print("correct version passes all edge cases:", all(max_subarray(c) == brute(c) for c in edge_cases() if c))
```

```console
$ PYTHONPATH=../lib python3 edge_cases.py
edge case [-3] exposes the bug: buggy=0, correct=-3
correct version passes all edge cases: True
```

The single-negative case exposes the classic Kadane bug (returning 0 when every element is negative) — exactly the cases a deliberate edge-case list includes and a "happy path" trace misses.

### Deep & Tricky

**DT-56. Complexity statements must name the variable and the case: "O(n log n) expected" (randomised quicksort), "O(1) amortised" (dynamic array append, DSU), "O(n + m)" (two inputs), "O(n·L) where L is the word length" (tries, hashing strings) — and hashing a string of length L costs O(L), not O(1).** *(CLRS ch. 17 on amortised analysis; Python data model: `hash(str)` reads every character on first use, then caches it)* A frequent interview slip is calling a dictionary of strings "O(1) per lookup" when the keys are long and fresh; another is ignoring the output size (generating all subsets is Ω(n·2ⁿ) just to write them). Say what n is, whether the bound is worst-case, amortised, or expected, and include the cost of the operations you treat as primitives.

## Topic 48B — Follow-ups

## Unit 48.3 — The standard follow-ups and how to answer them

**One-line summary:** Follow-ups probe whether you understand **why** your solution works, by changing one assumption. Prepare answers to the common ones:

| Follow-up | Typical answer |
| --- | --- |
| "What if n is 10⁹?" | The input cannot be stored or scanned per query: binary search on values, math, streaming, or sampling |
| "What if the data arrives as a stream?" | One pass, bounded memory: running aggregates, heaps of size k, reservoir sampling, sketches (Ch. 42) |
| "What if it does not fit in memory?" | External sorting/merging, hashing into partitions, sketches (this chapter's project) |
| "What if there are many queries?" | Preprocess once: prefix sums, sparse tables, segment trees, indexes (Ch. 18–19) |
| "What if values are updated?" | Fenwick/segment trees; balanced BSTs; lazy rebuilding |
| "Can you do it in O(1) extra space?" | In-place techniques: two pointers, cyclic sort, reversal, Floyd (Ch. 2, 8) |
| "Can you make it parallel / thread-safe?" | Partition the data, combine results (map–reduce); locks or confinement (Ch. 44) |
| "What if the input is adversarial?" | Randomised pivots and hash seeds (DT-50); worst-case guarantees |

```python
# file: stream_followup.py
import heapq
import random

def top_k_stream(stream, k):                          # follow-up: "the numbers arrive as a stream" -> heap of size k
    h = []
    for x in stream:
        if len(h) < k:
            heapq.heappush(h, x)
        elif x > h[0]:
            heapq.heapreplace(h, x)
    return sorted(h, reverse=True)

def running_mean_and_variance(stream):                 # Welford: numerically stable, O(1) memory
    n, mean, m2 = 0, 0.0, 0.0
    for x in stream:
        n += 1
        d = x - mean
        mean += d / n
        m2 += d * (x - mean)
    return mean, m2 / (n - 1) if n > 1 else 0.0

rng = random.Random(44)
data = (rng.gauss(10**9, 1) for _ in range(1_000_000))  # a generator: never materialised
print("top 3 of a million streamed values:", top_k_stream((rng.randint(0, 10**9) for _ in range(10**6)), 3))
mean, var = running_mean_and_variance(data)
print(f"Welford over 10^6 values near 1e9: mean {mean:.4f}, variance {var:.4f} (true variance 1)")
naive = [rng.gauss(10**9, 1) for _ in range(100_000)]
s, s2 = sum(naive), sum(x * x for x in naive)
print(f"naive E[x^2] - E[x]^2 on 10^5 values near 1e9: variance {s2 / len(naive) - (s / len(naive)) ** 2:.1f}  (catastrophic cancellation)")
```

```console
$ python3 stream_followup.py
top 3 of a million streamed values: [999997146, 999996848, 999995721]
Welford over 10^6 values near 1e9: mean 1000000000.0009, variance 1.0018 (true variance 1)
naive E[x^2] - E[x]^2 on 10^5 values near 1e9: variance -128.0  (catastrophic cancellation)
```

The variance follow-up is a favourite because the textbook formula E[x²] − E[x]² fails numerically when values are large relative to their spread; Welford's update stays accurate in one pass.

### Pattern

**P-49. In an interview: clarify → brute force with complexity → improved idea with its invariant (agree before coding) → clean code → deliberate edge-case tests → precise complexity → follow-ups. Think aloud about decisions, not keystrokes.** *(Practice)* Rehearse with a timer and someone (or a recording) listening; the gap between solving alone and solving while explaining is real and closes only with practice. *Trade-off:* spending time on clarification and a brute force feels slow, but it prevents the most expensive failure — a fast, confident solution to the wrong problem.

### Mastery check

1. **Predict.** What is the time complexity of inserting n strings of length L into a Python `set`, and why is it not O(n)?
2. **Predict.** Which edge case breaks a Kadane implementation that initialises `best = 0`?

## Chapter 48 Project — External merge sort: sorting more data than fits in memory

**Goal:** the classic system-design-flavoured follow-up — "sort a file of numbers that is larger than memory". Simulate a memory budget of M numbers: (1) read the input in chunks of M, sort each in memory, and write sorted **runs** to disk; (2) **k-way merge** the runs with a heap (Unit 15.3), reading each run sequentially through a small buffer. Verify the output against `sorted()` and count passes over the data: the I/O cost is about 2N·(1 + ⌈log_k(N/M)⌉) numbers read and written.

```python
# file: extsort/extsort.py
import heapq
import os
import random
import tempfile
import time

def write_numbers(path, nums):
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        f.write("\n".join(map(str, nums)) + ("\n" if nums else ""))

def read_numbers(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            yield int(line)

def external_sort(in_path, out_path, memory_numbers, tmpdir):
    runs, chunk, io = [], [], {"read": 0, "written": 0}
    def flush():
        chunk.sort()
        path = os.path.join(tmpdir, f"run{len(runs)}.txt")
        write_numbers(path, chunk)
        io["written"] += len(chunk)
        runs.append(path)
        chunk.clear()
    for x in read_numbers(in_path):                    # pass 1: sorted runs of size <= M
        io["read"] += 1
        chunk.append(x)
        if len(chunk) == memory_numbers:
            flush()
    if chunk:
        flush()
    readers = [read_numbers(p) for p in runs]           # pass 2: one k-way merge (k = number of runs)
    with open(out_path, "w") as out:
        for x in heapq.merge(*readers):                 # heap of run heads (Unit 15.3)
            io["read"] += 1
            out.write(f"{x}\n")
            io["written"] += 1
    return len(runs), io

rng = random.Random(45)
N, M = 1_000_000, 50_000
nums = [rng.randint(-10**12, 10**12) for _ in range(N)]
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    src, dst = os.path.join(d, "in.txt"), os.path.join(d, "out.txt")
    write_numbers(src, nums)
    t = time.perf_counter()
    nruns, io = external_sort(src, dst, M, d)
    el = time.perf_counter() - t
    ok = list(read_numbers(dst)) == sorted(nums)
print(f"N = {N:,} numbers, memory for {M:,}: {nruns} sorted runs, one {nruns}-way merge; "
      f"read {io['read']:,} and wrote {io['written']:,} numbers (2 passes); correct: {ok}  [{el:.1f} s]")
```

```console
$ cd extsort && python3 extsort.py
N = 1,000,000 numbers, memory for 50,000: 20 sorted runs, one 20-way merge; read 2,000,000 and wrote 2,000,000 numbers (2 passes); correct: True  [0.9 s]
```

With 20 runs, a single 20-way merge suffices, so the data is read and written twice in total. If the number of runs exceeded what can be merged at once (limited by memory for buffers, or by open-file limits), the merge would proceed in several passes — log_k(N/M) of them — which is why databases make runs as long as possible (replacement selection produces runs about 2M long on random input).

### Review checklist

- Why does the merge need memory only for one buffered element per run (plus the heap)?
- How many passes would be needed with N/M = 1,000 runs and at most 32 runs merged at once?
- How would you find the **median** of a file larger than memory without fully sorting it? (Selection by bucketing on value ranges, or a two-pass approach with counting.)

## Answers to the Chapter 48 prediction questions

**48.3 Q1.** O(n·L): each insertion hashes the whole string (O(L)) and, on a hash match, compares strings (up to O(L)). It is O(n) only if L is bounded by a constant.

**48.3 Q2.** An array of only negative numbers (e.g. [−3] or [−2, −1]): the true answer is the largest (least negative) element, but `best = 0` returns 0, the empty subarray, which the problem does not allow.

# Chapter 49 — Mock Interviews and a Study Plan

*Goal: rehearse complete interviews with realistic problems, hint ladders, and scoring rubrics; and organise your preparation into a concrete plan — which chapters, in which order, how many problems, and how to review — with spaced repetition so that patterns stay recognisable on the day.*

**What you will be able to do after this chapter**

- Run (or take) a mock interview with a rubric that matches how interviewers score.
- Use a hint ladder to practise getting unstuck productively.
- Follow a 12-week plan (or a compressed 4-week one) through this book.
- Schedule reviews with a Leitner-box spaced-repetition system over the book's DT and P entries.

## Topic 49A — Mock interviews

## Unit 49.1 — The rubric

**One-line summary:** Interviewers score four things, roughly equally: **problem solving** (did you find a correct, efficient approach, and how much help did you need?), **coding** (correct, clean, idiomatic), **verification** (did you test and find your own bugs?), and **communication** (could they follow your reasoning?). A correct optimal solution with silent coding and no testing can score lower than a slightly slower solution that was clearly explained and carefully tested.

| Score | Problem solving | Coding | Verification | Communication |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Strong | Optimal approach, independently, with justification | Correct first time or bugs self-found; clean structure | Chooses edge cases deliberately; traces precisely | Clarifies, explains trade-offs, invites input |
| Mixed | Optimal with one or two hints, or a near-optimal approach | Minor bugs found with prompting | Tests the happy path only | Explains when asked |
| Weak | Brute force only, or wrong approach | Incomplete or incorrect | No testing | Silent or unclear |

## Unit 49.2 — Six mock interviews

Each mock lists the problem, what a strong candidate asks, the expected progression, a **hint ladder** (give one hint at a time, only when the candidate is stuck for several minutes), and follow-ups. Run them with a friend acting as interviewer, 45 minutes each, and score with the rubric.

**Mock 1 — Subarray sum equals k** (warm-up, 25 minutes)
- *Problem:* count contiguous subarrays of an integer array (negatives allowed) whose sum is k.
- *Clarify:* negatives? (yes — this rules out sliding window); n up to 2·10⁵.
- *Progression:* O(n²) prefix differences → O(n) prefix sum + hash map counting earlier prefixes equal to P − k (Unit 2.2).
- *Hints:* (1) "What is the sum of a[i:j] in terms of prefix sums?" (2) "For a fixed j, which i work?" (3) "How can you count earlier prefixes with a given value quickly?"
- *Follow-ups:* return the longest such subarray; k changes per query; the array is a stream.

**Mock 2 — Course schedule with ordering** (graph, 45 minutes)
- *Problem:* n courses, prerequisite pairs; return an order to take all courses, or report impossible.
- *Clarify:* duplicates in prerequisites? self-loops? n up to 10⁵.
- *Progression:* repeatedly pick a course with no remaining prerequisites → Kahn's algorithm (Unit 21.1); impossible iff fewer than n output.
- *Hints:* (1) "Which course can you take first?" (2) "What changes after you take it?" (3) "How do you find the next available course without rescanning?"
- *Follow-ups:* the lexicographically smallest order (heap); minimum number of semesters (BFS layers); at most k courses per semester (NP-hard in general — bitmask DP for small n, card 61).

**Mock 3 — Minimise the largest sum when splitting an array into k parts** (binary search on the answer, 45 minutes)
- *Clarify:* non-negative values? (yes); n ≤ 10⁵, values ≤ 10⁴.
- *Progression:* DP O(k·n²) → observation: "can we split with max sum ≤ X?" is a greedy O(n) check and monotone in X → binary search on X between max(a) and sum(a) (Unit 6.3).
- *Hints:* (1) "If someone told you the answer X, could you verify it?" (2) "If X works, does X + 1?" (3) "What are the smallest and largest possible answers?"
- *Follow-ups:* negative numbers (the greedy check breaks — why?); output the split; very large k.

**Mock 4 — LRU cache** (design, 45 minutes)
- *Clarify:* capacity ≥ 1? what does get return for missing keys? thread safety required?
- *Progression:* list scan O(n) → hash map + doubly linked list O(1) (Unit 43.1); mention `OrderedDict`, then implement the linked list by hand if asked.
- *Hints:* (1) "Which operation is slow with just a dict?" (2) "Which structure removes an arbitrary element in O(1) given a pointer to it?"
- *Follow-ups:* LFU (Unit 43.2); TTL expiry; thread safety (one lock; or sharded caches).

**Mock 5 — Word break, return all sentences** (DP + backtracking, 45 minutes)
- *Clarify:* dictionary size, word lengths, output size limits.
- *Progression:* plain backtracking (exponential, repeated work) → memoise "all sentences of s[i:]" → note the output itself can be exponential; first check feasibility with the O(n·L) DP (Unit 28.4) to prune.
- *Hints:* (1) "Which suffixes are you solving repeatedly?" (2) "Can you know quickly that a suffix has no segmentation at all?"
- *Follow-ups:* count sentences modulo 10⁹+7 (no listing); dictionary of 10⁵ words (trie walk instead of slicing).

**Mock 6 — Median of a data stream with deletions** (hard, 45 minutes)
- *Problem:* support add(x), remove(x) (x present), and median() efficiently.
- *Progression:* sorted list O(n) per update → two heaps with lazy deletion and balance bookkeeping (Ch. 15 project) or an order-statistic structure (SortedList / treap, Ch. 14).
- *Hints:* (1) "Without deletions, how would you keep the median?" (2) "Heaps cannot delete arbitrary elements — can you delete later?" (3) "How do you know the true sizes of the heaps?"
- *Follow-ups:* percentile p instead of median; sliding window; distributed stream (approximate quantile sketches).

## Topic 49B — The plan

## Unit 49.3 — A 12-week plan through this book

**One-line summary:** About 8–10 hours per week: each week, read the units, code every pattern template from memory, solve 10–15 problems (half from the chapter, half mixed review), and run one timed session. Weeks 1–4 build the core, 5–8 the graph and DP depth, 9–10 the advanced topics, 11–12 mastery and mock interviews.

| Week | Chapters | Focus | Problems |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0–3 | method, complexity, arrays/prefix sums, hashing | 12 |
| 2 | 4–7 | two pointers, sliding window, binary search, sorting | 15 |
| 3 | 8–12 | lists, stacks, backtracking, bits, math | 15 |
| 4 | 13–16 | trees, BSTs, heaps, tries | 15 |
| 5 | 17–19 | DSU, segment trees, Fenwick trees | 12 |
| 6 | 20–23 | BFS/DFS, topological sort, shortest paths, MST | 15 |
| 7 | 24–27 | SCC/bridges, tree techniques, flows, Euler/Hamilton | 10 |
| 8 | 28–31 | DP foundations, sequence DP, knapsack, interval DP | 15 |
| 9 | 32–36 | tree/bitmask/digit DP, games, DP optimisations | 12 |
| 10 | 37–44 | greedy, sweeps, strings, geometry, D&C, randomised, design, concurrency | 15 |
| 11 | 45–47 | triage drill, combined problems, hard cards | 20 |
| 12 | 48–49 | interview craft, six mock interviews, review weak areas | 6 mocks |

**Compressed 4-week plan** (for an interview soon): Week 1: Chapters 0–7. Week 2: 13, 15, 17, 20–22. Week 3: 28–30, 37–38, 43. Week 4: 45–47 drills and four mock interviews. Skip flows, geometry, suffix structures, and DP optimisations unless the target company is known to ask them.

### Deep & Tricky

**DT-57. Spaced, retrieval-based practice beats massed re-reading: reviewing material at increasing intervals, by trying to recall it before looking, produces much better long-term retention than the same time spent re-reading in one block.** *(Cepeda et al., "Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks", Psychological Bulletin 132(3), 2006; Roediger & Karpicke, "Test-enhanced learning", Psychological Science 17(3), 2006)* For algorithms this means: close the book and re-derive the template (the invariant, the loop) from memory; solve an old problem again after a week, then after three weeks; and use the DT and P entries in Appendix A as flash cards. Re-reading a solution feels productive but mostly builds familiarity, not recall.

### Pattern

**P-50. Prepare like you will perform: timed, out loud, from memory, with a rubric. Mix new chapters with spaced review of old ones, keep a log of misses and their missed signals, and turn each miss into a card you will see again.** *(Practice)* Quantity matters less than deliberate review: 150 problems solved and reviewed beat 500 seen once. *Trade-off:* a plan only works if it is sustainable — fewer hours every week beat a heroic week followed by none.

### Mastery check

1. **Predict.** In the rubric, how would a silent candidate who writes an optimal, bug-free solution likely score on communication and verification?
2. **Predict.** In a Leitner system with boxes reviewed every 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 days, how many reviews does a card need, at minimum, to reach box 5?

## Chapter 49 Project — A Leitner-box scheduler for the book's DT and P entries

**Goal:** turn this book's 57 Deep & Tricky entries and 50 Patterns into a spaced-repetition deck. In a **Leitner system**, every card starts in box 1; a correct recall moves it up one box, a miss sends it back to box 1; box b is reviewed every 2^(b−1) days. Simulate 60 days for a learner who recalls a card with a probability that grows with its box, and report how many cards reach the top box and how many reviews it took — compared with reviewing every card every day.

```python
# file: leitner/leitner.py
import random

DT_COUNT, P_COUNT = 57, 50
cards = [f"DT-{i}" for i in range(1, DT_COUNT + 1)] + [f"P-{i}" for i in range(1, P_COUNT + 1)]
INTERVAL = {1: 1, 2: 2, 3: 4, 4: 8, 5: 16}

def recall_probability(box):                         # a simple learner model: stronger memory in higher boxes
    return {1: 0.55, 2: 0.70, 3: 0.82, 4: 0.90, 5: 0.95}[box]

def simulate(days, rng, daily_new=8):
    box, due, introduced, reviews = {}, {}, 0, 0
    for day in range(days):
        while introduced < len(cards) and introduced < (day + 1) * daily_new:
            c = cards[introduced]; box[c], due[c] = 1, day; introduced += 1
        for c in [c for c in box if due[c] <= day]:
            reviews += 1
            if rng.random() < recall_probability(box[c]):
                box[c] = min(5, box[c] + 1)
            else:
                box[c] = 1
            due[c] = day + INTERVAL[box[c]]
    return box, reviews

rng = random.Random(46)
box, reviews = simulate(60, rng)
dist = {b: sum(1 for v in box.values() if v == b) for b in range(1, 6)}
print(f"{len(cards)} cards (DT-1..DT-{DT_COUNT}, P-1..P-{P_COUNT}), 60 days, 8 new cards per day")
print("cards per box:", dist)
print(f"total reviews: {reviews:,} (about {reviews / 60:.0f} per day) vs reviewing every card daily: "
      f"{sum(min(len(cards), (d + 1) * 8) for d in range(60)):,}")
```

```console
$ cd leitner && python3 leitner.py
107 cards (DT-1..DT-57, P-1..P-50), 60 days, 8 new cards per day
cards per box: {1: 2, 2: 1, 3: 1, 4: 2, 5: 101}
total reviews: 1,077 (about 18 per day) vs reviewing every card daily: 5,757
```

Most cards climb to the high boxes, where they are seen only every 8–16 days, so the daily workload stays small while every card keeps being retrieved. Replace the simulated `recall_probability` with your honest self-assessment and you have a working review schedule for this book.

### Review checklist

- Why does a miss send a card back to box 1 rather than down one box, and what would change if it went down one box?
- How would you prioritise cards from chapters where your problem log shows the most misses?
- Which DT entries would you add from your own mistakes?

## Answers to the Chapter 49 prediction questions

**49.3 Q1.** Strong on problem solving and coding, but weak-to-mixed on communication and verification: the interviewer cannot see the reasoning or the testing, so those dimensions lack evidence — often enough to turn a "strong hire" into a "lean hire".

**49.3 Q2.** Four correct recalls in a row (box 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5), taking at least 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 days.

# Appendix A — Index of Deep & Tricky entries and Patterns

Every *Deep & Tricky* entry (DT) and *Pattern* (P) in the book, in number order, with the unit where it is explained. Use it for revision: read each title and explain the entry before looking it up.

## Deep & Tricky

| # | Entry | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DT-1 | Big-O hides constants and Python magnifies them: an O(n log n) solution using built-ins can beat an O(n) solution written as a Python loop. | Unit 0.2 |
| DT-2 | Amortised O(1) is not worst-case O(1): one operation can still take Θ(n), and that matters for latency. | Unit 1.3 |
| DT-3 | Recursion that recomputes overlapping subproblems is exponential, and the fix — memoisation — turns T(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−2) into Θ(n). | Unit 1.4 |
| DT-4 | Forgetting the empty prefix (`count[0] = 1`, or `first = {0: -1}`) silently misses every subarray that starts at index 0. | Unit 2.2 |
| DT-5 | In Python, `-7 % 3 == 2`, but in C, C++, Java, and JavaScript, `-7 % 3 == -1`. | Unit 2.2 |
| DT-6 | A `while` loop inside a `for` loop is still O(n) when each inner iteration permanently fixes something. | Unit 2.6 |
| DT-7 | With k = 0, "look up x − k and x + k" counts every equal pair twice — special cases hide in the symmetry of the complement. | Unit 3.2 |
| DT-8 | The birthday paradox makes hash collisions far more likely than 1/M suggests: with m distinct strings, expect a collision once m ≈ √M. | Unit 3.5 |
| DT-9 | Python's own `hash()` is fine for dictionaries but useless as a rolling hash — and `hash(-1) == hash(-2)`. | Unit 3.5 |
| DT-10 | "Container with most water" moves the *shorter* side because the area is limited by it: any narrower container using the shorter side is strictly worse. | Unit 4.1 |
| DT-11 | A sliding window over sums needs non-negative numbers; with negatives the window is not monotone and the algorithm is wrong. | Unit 5.2 |
| DT-12 | `lo = mid` with `mid = (lo + hi) // 2` loops forever when `hi = lo + 1` — always pair the update with the rounding direction. | Unit 6.1 |
| DT-13 | Quicksort with a fixed pivot (first or last element) is Θ(n²) on sorted input — and with two-way partitioning, on arrays of equal elements too. | Unit 7.1 |
| DT-14 | A comparator must define a consistent total order — transitive and antisymmetric — or sorting may produce garbage (or, in Java, throw "Comparison method violates its general contract!"). | Unit 7.3 |
| DT-15 | Floyd's algorithm works on any function f from a finite set to itself: the sequence x, f(x), f(f(x)), … is a "rho"-shaped linked list. | Unit 8.2 |
| DT-16 | When counting "subarrays where a[i] is the minimum", equal values must be broken asymmetrically — strict on one side, non-strict on the other — or subarrays with repeated minimums are counted twice or not at all. | Unit 9.3 |
| DT-17 | Python's default recursion limit (1000) is a guard, not a stack size; raising it with `sys.setrecursionlimit` can turn a clean `RecursionError` into a hard crash of the interpreter. | Unit 10.1 |
| DT-18 | In `permute_unique`, the condition `not used[i - 1]` (not `used[i - 1]`) forces equal values to be placed in their original left-to-right order; either condition removes duplicates, but this one prunes at the top of the tree and is much faster. | Unit 10.3 |
| DT-19 | Python integers have unbounded width and behave as if they had infinitely many sign bits: `-1 >> 5 == -1`, `~5 == -6`, and `bin(-6)` prints `-0b110`, not a two's-complement bit pattern. | Unit 11.1 |
| DT-20 | Under a modulus, "a / b" is not `(a % p) // (b % p)` — it is `a · b⁻¹ mod p`, and the inverse exists only when gcd(b, p) = 1. | Unit 12.3 |
| DT-21 | The one-pass LCA function assumes both p and q are in the tree; if one is missing, it returns the other instead of "no LCA". | Unit 13.4 |
| DT-22 | In Python, `bisect.insort` into a list is O(n) per insertion — but the O(n) is a `memmove` in C, so for n up to ~10⁵ it often beats a pure-Python O(log n) tree; `sortedcontainers.SortedList` exploits this with a list of sorted sublists. | Unit 14.4 |
| DT-23 | `heapify` is O(n), not O(n log n): sifting down from the last parent to the root costs at most the node's height, and most nodes are near the bottom — Σ height ≈ n. | Unit 15.1 |
| DT-24 | Without output (dictionary) links, Aho–Corasick reports only the longest pattern ending at each position — or, if you walk the full failure chain at every character, it degrades to O(¦text¦ · depth). | Unit 16.4 |
| DT-25 | Path compression and union by size together give O(α(n)) amortised per operation, and this bound is tight: no pointer-based union–find can do better in the worst case. | Unit 17.1 |
| DT-26 | The bottom-up iterative query is correct for non-commutative operations only if the left and right accumulators are kept separately and combined as `left ⊕ right` at the end; for n not a power of two, the "tree" is a forest, and order is still preserved by this scheme. | Unit 18.1 |
| DT-27 | A sparse table's O(1) query relies on idempotence (x ⊕ x = x): the two blocks overlap, so the overlap is counted twice. For sums, overlapping blocks give wrong answers; use O(log n) disjoint blocks or prefix sums instead. | Unit 19.4 |
| DT-28 | Marking a vertex as visited when it is dequeued instead of when it is enqueued keeps BFS correct but can make it quadratic (or exponential in memory on dense graphs): the same vertex is enqueued once per incoming edge from the current frontier. | Unit 20.2 |
| DT-29 | For directed graphs, "visited" with two states is not enough to detect cycles: an edge to an already-visited vertex may be a harmless cross or forward edge. Only an edge to a vertex still on the current path (gray) proves a cycle. | Unit 21.2 |
| DT-30 | Dijkstra's algorithm is wrong with negative edge weights even when there is no negative cycle: a settled vertex can later be reached more cheaply through a negative edge, and the lazy version may either return wrong distances or, if it re-relaxes settled vertices, take exponential time. | Unit 22.1 |
| DT-31 | If all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique; with ties there can be many MSTs, but they all have the same total weight and the same multiset of edge weights. | Unit 23.2 |
| DT-32 | In the low-link computation for bridges, the edge to skip is the specific edge you arrived by, not "the parent vertex": with parallel edges between p and v, the second copy is a genuine back edge, and neither copy is a bridge. | Unit 24.2 |
| DT-33 | Heavy–light decomposition's O(log n) bound counts *light edges* on a path, not chains: moving up a light edge from v to its parent p means size[p] ≥ 2·size[v], so at most log₂ n light edges lie on any root path. | Unit 25.5 |
| DT-34 | Max-flow = min-cut, and after a maximum flow the set S of vertices reachable from s in the residual graph defines a minimum cut: every edge from S to its complement is saturated, and every edge back into S carries zero flow. | Unit 26.1 |
| DT-35 | Eulerian path is in P (linear time), while Hamiltonian path is NP-complete; the problems look almost identical, so classify carefully: "every edge once" is Euler, "every vertex once" is Hamilton. | Unit 27.4 |
| DT-36 | DP is correct only if the state captures everything the future depends on (the Markov property); if two different histories reach the "same" state but have different futures, memoising on that state returns wrong answers — silently. | Unit 28.4 |
| DT-37 | `tails` in the O(n log n) LIS is not itself an increasing subsequence of the input — only its length is meaningful; reconstructing requires parent pointers recorded at insertion time. | Unit 29.1 |
| DT-38 | In the one-row knapsack, the loop direction *is* the semantics: backwards = each item at most once (0/1), forwards = unlimited reuse; and for counting, the order of the two loops decides combinations versus permutations. | Unit 30.2 |
| DT-39 | In burst balloons, defining k as the balloon burst *first* gives a wrong recurrence: after k bursts, its neighbours become adjacent, so the left and right parts are no longer independent; defining k as the balloon burst *last* in the open interval (i, j) keeps i and j as fixed neighbours and makes the parts independent. | Unit 31.2 |
| DT-40 | "At least one child in state X" cannot be written as a plain sum over children; compute the sum with each child's best allowed state, then add the cheapest *penalty* for forcing one child into X. | Unit 32.2 |
| DT-41 | SOS DP is the n-dimensional prefix sum over the boolean hypercube: each bit is one dimension of size 2, and summing dimension by dimension is the same trick as building a 2-D prefix sum row by row, then column by column. | Unit 33.4 |
| DT-42 | In digit DP, `tight` must be passed as `tight and d == limit`, and the memo must include it — but most of the work happens in non-tight states, which are shared across all bounds of the same length; forgetting `started` silently counts leading zeros as real digits. | Unit 34.2 |
| DT-43 | Backward expectation DP needs an acyclic state graph; if transitions can return to earlier states (snakes, retries, random walks), "E[s] depends on E[s]" and the DP has no valid order — the expectations satisfy a linear system instead, which must be solved. | Unit 35.2 |
| DT-44 | Divide-and-conquer and Knuth optimisations are valid only when the cost function satisfies the quadrangle inequality (C(a, c) + C(b, d) ≤ C(a, d) + C(b, c) for a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ d) or an equivalent monotonicity of optimal split points; applied to a cost that violates it, they return wrong answers with no error. | Unit 36.3 |
| DT-45 | A greedy algorithm is optimal exactly when the problem has the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure; matroids characterise a large family of such problems (maximum-weight independent sets in a matroid are found by sorting and adding greedily), but many greedy-looking problems — coin change with arbitrary denominations, 0/1 knapsack — are not matroids and greedy fails. | Unit 37.1 |
| DT-46 | Whether intervals that only touch ([1, 3] and [3, 5]) overlap depends on whether they are closed or half-open, and the sweep must order simultaneous events accordingly: for half-open [s, e), process ends before starts at the same coordinate; for closed [s, e], starts before ends. | Unit 38.1 |
| DT-47 | KMP and the Z-function are O(n) because a pointer that only moves forward (the matched length in KMP, the right end r of the Z-box) bounds the total work; Python's built-in `str.find` is not guaranteed linear and, on adversarial inputs, older CPython versions could be quadratic. | Unit 39.2 |
| DT-48 | Floating-point orientation tests are not robust: near-collinear points can get inconsistent answers for cross(a, b, c), cross(b, c, a), and cross(c, a, b), and algorithms built on them (convex hull, intersection) can crash or return non-convex "hulls". | Unit 40.1 |
| DT-49 | Meet in the middle turns time 2ⁿ into 2^(n/2) but needs 2^(n/2) memory — and the combine step must be sub-quadratic in the half-lists (sorting + binary search or two pointers), or the gain disappears. | Unit 41.3 |
| DT-50 | In CPython, `hash(n)` for an `int` is n mod (2⁶¹ − 1) (on 64-bit builds), deterministic across runs; only `str` and `bytes` hashes are randomised. Keys that are multiples of 2⁶¹ − 1 all collide, and a dict of n such keys takes O(n²) time to build. | Unit 42.3 |
| DT-51 | In an LFU cache, the minimum frequency can only change in two ways: it becomes 1 when a new key is inserted, and it increases by exactly 1 when the last key of the minimum bucket is accessed — so it can be maintained in O(1) without a heap. | Unit 43.2 |
| DT-52 | The GIL guarantees that individual bytecode instructions do not interleave, but compound operations — `x += 1` on an attribute, `d[k] = d.get(k, 0) + 1`, check-then-act sequences — span several instructions and can be interrupted between them; in CPython 3.13 a plain `self.n += 1` rarely shows a race only because thread switches happen at specific points, not because it is atomic. | Unit 44.1 |
| DT-53 | Constraints are upper bounds chosen by the problem setter to let the intended complexity pass and slower ones fail — so they reveal the intended algorithm, but Python's constant factor (10–100× slower than C++) can shift the boundary by one row; and a "sum of n over all test cases ≤ 2·10⁵" constraint means the per-test bound is not what matters. | Unit 45.1 |
| DT-54 | "Offline" processing — reading all queries first and answering them in a convenient order — is often the key that turns an impossible online problem into a standard one, and it is allowed whenever the problem gives all queries up front; but the answers must be written back in the original query order. | Unit 46.2 |
| DT-55 | In "max sum ≤ k" problems, the answer may not exist (every rectangle exceeds k), and returning 0 or −∞ silently differs from the problem's convention; likewise, in "max points on a line", duplicates of the anchor lie on every line through it and must be added to every bucket, not counted as a direction. | Unit 47.3 |
| DT-56 | Complexity statements must name the variable and the case: "O(n log n) expected" (randomised quicksort), "O(1) amortised" (dynamic array append, DSU), "O(n + m)" (two inputs), "O(n·L) where L is the word length" (tries, hashing strings) — and hashing a string of length L costs O(L), not O(1). | Unit 48.2 |
| DT-57 | Spaced, retrieval-based practice beats massed re-reading: reviewing material at increasing intervals, by trying to recall it before looking, produces much better long-term retention than the same time spent re-reading in one block. | Unit 49.3 |

## Patterns

| # | Pattern | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P-1 | Write the brute force first; stress-test the optimised solution against it on small random inputs. | Unit 0.3 |
| P-2 | State the complexity of every solution — time *and* space, worst case *and* what dominates — before writing code. | Unit 1.6 |
| P-3 | Turn "range" questions into "difference of two prefixes" questions. | Unit 2.7 |
| P-4 | Default to a hash map; ask what the key should be. | Unit 3.5 |
| P-5 | Before writing two pointers, write the elimination argument: "when the condition is X, the element at pointer P cannot be in any remaining answer, because…". | Unit 4.5 |
| P-6 | Sliding window = two pointers + an aggregate that can be updated in O(1) when one element enters or leaves. | Unit 5.5 |
| P-7 | "Minimise the maximum" or "maximise the minimum" almost always means binary search on the answer with a greedy check. | Unit 6.5 |
| P-8 | When stuck, sort — and ask what sorted order makes easy. | Unit 7.5 |
| P-9 | Draw the pointers before and after every rewiring step, and save `next` before you overwrite it. | Unit 8.4 |
| P-10 | "Nearest element to the left/right that is greater/smaller" means a monotonic stack; "best element within a sliding range" means a monotonic deque. | Unit 9.6 |
| P-11 | Backtracking = choose / explore / un-choose, with state that is cheap to update and undo, and pruning as early (as high in the tree) as possible. | Unit 10.5 |
| P-12 | When a problem says "XOR", "subsets of n ≤ 20", "appears twice/three times", or "power of two", think bits: cancellation for XOR, bitmask for sets, per-bit counting for modular counts, and high-to-low greedy for maximising XOR. | Unit 11.4 |
| P-13 | Keep arithmetic exact: integers and modular arithmetic for counts, `fractions.Fraction` or cross-multiplication for ratios, and `math.isqrt` instead of `int(x  | Unit 12.4 |
| P-14 | For a tree problem, first decide: does the answer flow up (return a summary from children — postorder) or down (pass state from the root — preorder)? If a path can bend at a node, compute the bent answer into a global while returning the straight one. | Unit 13.5 |
| P-15 | When a problem needs "the k-th smallest so far", "how many are smaller than x", or "nearest value above/below x" under insertions and deletions, reach for an ordered multiset: a balanced BST with sizes in theory, `SortedList` (or `bisect` on a list for small n) in Python. | Unit 14.4 |
| P-16 | "Repeatedly need the minimum/maximum of a changing set" → heap. "Top k" → heap of size k with the *opposite* order. "Median" → two heaps. "Merge sorted things" → heap of frontiers. | Unit 15.5 |
| P-17 | Many strings sharing prefixes → trie; many patterns against one text → Aho–Corasick; XOR maximisation over a set → binary trie. | Unit 16.4 |
| P-18 | "Are these connected?", "how many groups?", "merge groups sharing X", with edges arriving over time → DSU. Relations relative to a group (ratios, differences, parity) → weighted DSU. Deletions known in advance → reverse time. | Unit 17.5 |
| P-19 | Range query + updates → segment tree. Decide the node data by asking "what do I need from two adjacent halves to answer for their union?", then the identity, then (for range updates) how tags apply to a node and compose with each other. | Unit 18.5 |
| P-20 | Choose the lightest tool: no updates and invertible op → prefix sums; no updates and idempotent op → sparse table; point updates and prefix-style queries → Fenwick; anything else with updates → segment tree; offline queries with an O(1) add/remove → Mo's. | Unit 19.5 |
| P-21 | "Minimum number of steps/moves" with all moves costing the same → BFS over states. "Can I reach / how many groups / fill a region" → DFS or BFS, whichever is easier to write. Always ask: what is the full state, and how many states are there? | Unit 20.5 |
| P-22 | Dependencies → directed graph → topological order (Kahn for simplicity and cycle detection by count; DFS when you need the cycle itself). Any "best/count over paths" in a DAG → DP in topological order. | Unit 21.4 |
| P-23 | Pick the shortest-path algorithm from the weights: unit → BFS, {0, 1} → 0-1 BFS, non-negative → Dijkstra, negative → Bellman–Ford (or DAG DP if acyclic), all pairs on small V → Floyd–Warshall, single target with geometry → A*. Extra constraints (stops, fuel, coupons, parity) become extra state components. | Unit 22.5 |
| P-24 | "Connect everything at minimum total cost" → MST: Kruskal for sparse edge lists (and when you also want components or thresholds), dense Prim for complete graphs given as points. "Minimise the largest edge on a path" → MST / Kruskal until connected. | Unit 23.3 |
| P-25 | Directed "mutual reachability", cycles of dependencies, or "condense loops then reason on a DAG" → SCC. Undirected "single points of failure" → bridges / articulation points via low-links. Binary choices with pairwise constraints → 2-SAT. | Unit 24.3 |
| P-26 | On trees: subtree questions → Euler tour + range structure; path questions with updates → HLD; ancestor/LCA/distance → binary lifting (or Euler tour + RMQ); "for every root" → rerooting; "count or optimise over all paths" or "nearest marked vertex" → centroid decomposition. | Unit 25.6 |
| P-27 | If a problem asks for a maximum number of disjoint things, an assignment respecting capacities, or a minimum set of edges/vertices whose removal separates two parts — try to draw it as a flow network. Matching → bipartite flow; "choose items with prerequisites to maximise profit" → min cut; "assign at minimum cost" → min-cost flow or Hungarian. | Unit 26.4 |
| P-28 | "Every edge exactly once" → check degrees, then Hierholzer. "Every vertex exactly once" with n ≤ ~18 → bitmask DP (dp[mask][last]). Colouring with 2 colours → BFS; with k colours on small n → backtracking or subset DP; large graphs → greedy heuristics with good orderings. | Unit 27.4 |
| P-29 | For any DP: write the state's meaning in one sentence, derive the transition from "the last choice", list base cases, choose an order (or memoise), and identify the answer state. Then estimate states × transitions before coding. | Unit 28.5 |
| P-30 | One sequence → state "ending at i" (LIS-like) or "prefix i" (house-robber-like). Two sequences → state (i, j) over prefixes, transitions from matching or skipping the last characters. Grids → state (r, c), transitions from neighbours already computed. | Unit 29.5 |
| P-31 | Choices over items with a budget → knapsack. Each item once → backwards loop; unlimited → forwards; limited counts → binary splitting; several budgets → one dimension per budget; giant weights → index by value instead. Booleans in Python → big-integer bitsets. | Unit 30.4 |
| P-32 | Operations on adjacent elements whose cost depends on the range → interval DP over `[i, j]` by increasing length. Choose k as the split point or as the element handled last, so the two sides are independent. Two-player games on a row → score-difference DP. | Unit 31.4 |
| P-33 | Tree DP: decide the per-vertex state vector (taken/not, covered/not, how many used), write how a parent's state combines children's states (sums for optimisation, products for counting), and process vertices in reverse BFS order. | Unit 32.4 |
| P-34 | n ≤ 20 items whose *set* matters → bitmask state; order matters too → (mask, last); grouping items → submask DP (n ≤ ~15) or the (count, fill) trick; aggregates over all submasks → SOS; grids with narrow width → broken profile. | Unit 33.5 |
| P-35 | Huge numeric range + property of digits → digit DP over (position, tight, started, state); range answers via f(R) − f(L − 1); sums via (count, sum) pairs; k-th element via descending through counts. | Unit 34.3 |
| P-36 | Random processes on a DAG of states → forward probability DP or backward expectation DP; with cycles → linear system. "Expected number of …" → first try linearity over indicators. Two-player perfect-information games → win/lose DP or minimax; impartial games made of independent parts → Grundy numbers and XOR. | Unit 35.4 |
| P-37 | When a DP is correct but too slow, look at the transition's shape: a sliding window of states → monotonic deque; a minimum of linear functions of the current index → convex hull trick / Li Chao; layered partition DPs with monotone optimal splits → divide and conquer; interval DPs with quadrangle-inequality costs → Knuth; the same linear step repeated n times with huge n → matrix power. | Unit 36.5 |
| P-38 | Suspect greedy when a problem asks for a maximum count or minimum cost and some ordering (by end time, deadline, ratio, size) seems natural. Then: (1) write the brute force, (2) stress-test the candidate rule, (3) if it survives, find the exchange argument. | Unit 37.3 |
| P-39 | Intervals → sort by start (merging, inserting) or by end (selecting, stabbing). Questions about "at any moment" → events + sweep, with a counter for overlaps, a heap or ordered multiset for the best active item, and a segment tree for aggregates over coordinates. | Unit 38.4 |
| P-40 | Single-pattern search → `str.find` (or KMP/Z when you need borders, periods, or guarantees); many patterns → Aho–Corasick (Chapter 16); palindromes → Manacher; questions about all substrings (distinct count, repeats, common substrings, k-th substring) → suffix array + LCP or suffix automaton; quick probabilistic answers → rolling hash + binary search (Chapter 3). | Unit 39.5 |
| P-41 | Geometry: keep coordinates integral and decide everything with cross and dot products; sort and sweep for pair problems; reduce "extreme" questions to the convex hull; handle collinear, coincident, and touching cases explicitly and test them with tiny coordinate ranges. | Unit 40.4 |
| P-42 | If combining two halves' answers is cheap (linear after sorting), divide and conquer gives O(n log n); count cross pairs while merging. If n is around 30–40 and the objective is additive, split the items, enumerate each half, sort one, and search it from the other — meet in the middle. | Unit 41.3 |
| P-43 | Use randomness to (1) break worst cases (random pivots, random hash seeds), (2) sample fairly (Fisher–Yates, reservoir), (3) test quickly with bounded error (Miller–Rabin, polynomial identity testing), and (4) summarise huge streams in small memory (Bloom, Count-Min, HyperLogLog) — always stating the error guarantee. | Unit 42.4 |
| P-44 | For a design problem, write the operation list with target complexities, assign one structure per access path (map for key lookup, linked list/ordered dict for recency, buckets for frequency, array for random access, sorted list for time), and update all of them together in every operation. Test the whole class against a slow model with random operation sequences. | Unit 43.4 |
| P-45 | Shared mutable state + threads → identify every compound operation on it and protect it with one lock (or confine the state to one thread and communicate through a queue). Ordering between threads → events/semaphores for simple signals, condition variables with `while` loops for predicates. Several locks → a global acquisition order. | Unit 44.5 |
| P-46 | Recognition protocol: constraints → feasible complexity; signal phrases → two or three candidate patterns; brute force → oracle; candidate's invariant → hand check → stress test. Only then optimise. | Unit 45.3 |
| P-47 | For a hard problem, name the frame first (binary search on the answer, offline sweep in sorted order, DP over sorted items, enumerate the rate-setter), then the engine each frame step needs (BFS/DSU check, Fenwick/segment-tree range query, heap of best k). If two frames work, implement both and let them test each other. | Unit 46.5 |
| P-48 | When you meet a new hard problem, write its card: signals → insight → algorithm and complexity → trap → closest template. If you cannot fill "insight", you have not solved it yet — return to the brute force and look for the structure the brute force wastes. | Unit 47.5 |
| P-49 | In an interview: clarify → brute force with complexity → improved idea with its invariant (agree before coding) → clean code → deliberate edge-case tests → precise complexity → follow-ups. Think aloud about decisions, not keystrokes. | Unit 48.3 |
| P-50 | Prepare like you will perform: timed, out loud, from memory, with a rubric. Mix new chapters with spaced review of old ones, keep a log of misses and their missed signals, and turn each miss into a card you will see again. | Unit 49.3 |

# Appendix B — The Python Toolkit for Algorithms

This appendix collects the standard-library tools used throughout the book, with their costs and traps. All complexities are for CPython.

## Built-in containers

| Operation | list | dict / set | deque | str |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| index / lookup | `a[i]` O(1) | `d[k]`, `x in s` O(1) average | `q[i]` O(n) | `s[i]` O(1) |
| append / add | `append` O(1) amortised | O(1) average | `append`, `appendleft` O(1) | `+` creates a new string: O(n) |
| pop end | `pop()` O(1) | `popitem()` O(1) | `pop()`, `popleft()` O(1) | — |
| insert / delete in the middle | O(n) (`memmove`, fast) | O(1) | O(n) | O(n) |
| slice | O(k) copy | — | — | O(k) copy |
| sort | `sort()` O(n log n), stable (Timsort) | — | — | — |

- Build strings with `"".join(parts)`, never `s += piece` in a loop.
- `x in list` is O(n); convert to a set when testing membership repeatedly.
- `[[0] * C] * R` creates R references to **one** row; use `[[0] * C for _ in range(R)]`.

## `collections`

- `deque` — queues and sliding windows (Ch. 5, 20). `deque(maxlen=k)` keeps the last k items.
- `Counter` — counting (Ch. 3); `most_common(k)` uses a heap; `c1 - c2` drops non-positive counts.
- `defaultdict(list)` — adjacency lists and grouping.
- `OrderedDict` — `move_to_end`, `popitem(last=False)`: LRU caches (Unit 43.1).

## `heapq` (Chapter 15)

- Min-heap on a plain list: `heappush`, `heappop`, `heapify` (O(n)), `heapreplace`, `heappushpop`, `nsmallest`, `nlargest`, `merge`.
- Max-heap: push negated keys. Custom priority: push `(priority, counter, item)` so items are never compared.
- No decrease-key and no arbitrary delete: push duplicates and skip stale entries (Dijkstra, Unit 22.1), or use lazy deletion (Ch. 15 project).

## `bisect` (Chapters 6, 14)

- `bisect_left(a, x)` — first index with `a[i] >= x`; `bisect_right(a, x)` — first index with `a[i] > x`.
- `insort(a, x)` — O(n) insertion, fast in practice for n up to ~10⁵ (DT-22).
- Python 3.10+: `key=` parameter for searching by a derived key.

## `functools` and `itertools`

- `@cache` / `@lru_cache(maxsize=None)` — memoisation (Ch. 28). Arguments must be hashable (tuples, not lists). `f.cache_clear()` between test cases.
- `cmp_to_key` — sort with a comparison function (Unit 7.4).
- `reduce`, `accumulate` (prefix sums: `list(accumulate(a, initial=0))`), `pairwise` (3.10+), `product`, `permutations`, `combinations`, `combinations_with_replacement`, `islice`, `chain.from_iterable`.

## `math` and integers

- `math.gcd`, `math.lcm` (3.9+), `math.isqrt` (exact integer square root), `math.comb`, `math.perm`, `math.inf`.
- `pow(a, b, m)` — fast modular power; `pow(a, -1, m)` — modular inverse (3.8+) (Unit 12.3).
- `int.bit_length()`, `int.bit_count()` (3.10+) (Ch. 11). Integers are unbounded; bitwise operations on negatives behave as infinite two's complement (DT-19).
- `fractions.Fraction` for exact ratios (P-13); `decimal.Decimal` for controlled precision (Ch. 33 project).

## Recursion and speed

- Default recursion limit 1000 (DT-17): convert deep recursions to explicit stacks, or process trees in reversed BFS order (Unit 25.1).
- Fast input for large data: `data = sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()`.
- Local variable lookups are faster than global or attribute lookups; in hot loops, bind `append = out.append`.
- About 10⁷ simple operations per second (Unit 0.2): check the budget before coding (Unit 45.1).

## Third-party: `sortedcontainers`

- `SortedList` — `add`, `remove`, `bisect_left`, `bisect_right`, indexing `s[k]` (k-th smallest), `irange`, `islice`; all about O(log n), fast in practice (Ch. 14).
- `SortedDict`, `SortedSet` — ordered maps and sets (Ch. 38 project).
- Not in the standard library: in interviews, say you would use it, and be ready to explain the balanced-BST alternative.

## Data structures

| Dynamic array | O(1) index | O(1) amortised at end | O(n) middle | cache-friendly | 1, 2 |
| Hash map / set | O(1) average | O(1) average | O(1) average | O(n) worst case; adversarial keys (DT-50) | 3 |
| Linked list | O(n) | O(1) at a known node | O(1) at a known node | | 8 |
| Stack / queue / deque | O(1) ends | O(1) | O(1) | | 9 |
| Monotonic stack / deque | — | O(1) amortised | O(1) amortised | nearest greater/smaller; window max | 5, 9 |
| Binary heap | O(1) min | O(log n) | O(log n) pop | `heapify` O(n) | 15 |
| Balanced BST / treap | O(log n) search, rank, select | O(log n) | O(log n) | order statistics | 14 |
| Trie | O(L) | O(L) | O(L) | L = key length | 16 |
| Union–find | O(α(n)) find | — | — | union O(α(n)); no split | 17 |

| Fenwick tree | O(log n) prefix | O(log n) point update | — | invertible operations | 19 |
| Sparse table | O(1) idempotent range query | — | — | static; O(n log n) build | 19 |
| Suffix array + LCP | O(m log n) pattern search | — | — | O(n log n) build here | 39 |
| Suffix automaton | O(m) substring test | O(1) amortised per char | — | ≤ 2n − 1 states | 39 |
| Bloom filter | O(k) query | O(k) | — | false positives only | 42 |
| Count-Min sketch | O(d) | O(d) | — | overestimates only | 42 |

## Input size → target complexity

See Unit 45.1. In Python, divide the operation budget by about ten compared with C++.
